title: Matrix Compression via Randomized Low Rank and Low Precision Factorization
authors: Rajarshi Saha¹, Varun Srivastava¹, Mert Pilanci¹
title_audio_script: Modern matrices can hold billions of entries, making them expensive to store and process, yet they are often approximately low rank. This work from Stanford introduces LPLR, a randomized algorithm that factorizes any matrix into a product of two low-rank factors whose entries are also quantized to low precision. By combining low rank and low precision in a single step, LPLR compresses matrices down to about one bit per coordinate while matching or beating traditional compression on image reconstruction, embedding classification, and compressing the weights of LlaMa-7b.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.necessary: Modern matrices can contain billions of entries, making storage and computation costly, even though such matrices are often approximately low rank.
sections.additional: Low-rank approximation alone or low-precision quantization alone each leaves compression on the table; the two structures are rarely exploited jointly with error guarantees.
sections.audio_script: Matrices are the workhorse data structure across science and machine learning, but modern ones can involve billions of elements, and storing or processing them strains memory and compute. Fortunately, many real-world matrices are approximately low rank, carrying far less information than their size suggests. Prior work has exploited either the low-rank structure or low-precision quantization on its own, but combining both into a single compressed factorization, with provable error control, has remained open.

sections.heading: Motivation
sections.necessary: Compressing a matrix by both factorizing it into low-rank factors and quantizing those factors can multiply the savings, but naive combinations lose accuracy fast at aggressive bit budgets.
sections.additional: Computing a full SVD is O(nd²) and infeasible for very large matrices on current GPUs, so a cheaper randomized route to low-rank-plus-low-precision factors is needed.
sections.audio_script: If a matrix is low rank, we can write it as a product of a tall factor and a wide factor with far fewer entries than the original. If we then store those entries in low precision, we save even more. The catch is that doing this crudely, especially at very low bit budgets, degrades accuracy quickly, and the exact route through a singular value decomposition costs order n d squared computation, which is prohibitive for the largest matrices. The paper is motivated by finding a fast, randomized way to obtain low-rank and low-precision factors together while keeping the approximation error small and analyzable.

sections.heading: Contribution
sections.necessary: The paper introduces LPLR, a randomized algorithm that jointly produces a low-rank and low-precision factorization A ≈ LR, derives upper bounds on its approximation error as a function of target rank and bit budget, and demonstrates it on images, embeddings, and LLM weights.
sections.additional: It also proposes LPLR-SVD (LSVD), an SVD-based variant, and characterizes when direct-SVD quantization versus LPLR is preferable through the row-norm versus entry-bounded regimes (Tables 1 and 2).
sections.audio_script: The core contribution is LPLR, short for Low-Precision Low-Rank factorization, a randomized algorithm that simultaneously exploits low-rank structure and quantizes the resulting factors to low precision. The authors derive rigorous upper bounds on the approximation error, showing how it depends on the target rank and the quantization bit budget, and they expose a clean tradeoff between compression ratio and accuracy that practitioners can tune. They also introduce an SVD-based variant called LPLR-SVD, and they validate everything empirically on image compression, nearest-neighbor classification of image and text embeddings, and compression of the weight matrices of LlaMa-7b.

sections.heading: Method
sections.necessary: LPLR sketches the columns of A with a Gaussian matrix S to get an approximate range basis AS, quantizes it to Q(AS), then solves a least-squares projection W* = argmin ‖Q(AS)W − A‖²_F and quantizes W* to Q'(W*), returning L = Q(AS) and R = Q'(W*).
sections.additional: Because S is a Gaussian JL embedding, uniform quantization enjoys an equalization property: the vector quantization error of x̂ = SᵀQ(Sx) stays O(1) rather than growing as O(d), which is why LPLR tolerates aggressive bit budgets, even 1-bit sign quantization.
sections.audio_script: LPLR works in a few steps. First it draws a Gaussian sketching matrix S and forms the sketch A times S, which is a randomized rangefinder that approximates the column space of A. It quantizes this basis to get Q of A S. Then it computes the least-squares projection of the columns of A onto this quantized basis, solving for W star that minimizes the Frobenius norm of Q of A S times W minus A, a problem with the closed form W star equals the pseudoinverse of Q of A S times A, or solvable iteratively by conjugate gradients. Finally it quantizes W star with a second quantizer, and returns the two factors: L equals the quantized basis and R equals the quantized projection. A key insight is that Gaussian sketches are Johnson-Lindenstrauss embeddings with an equalization property, so the quantization error of the reconstruction stays order one and does not grow with dimension, which is exactly why LPLR remains accurate even at one bit per coordinate.

sections.heading: Dataset / Benchmark
sections.necessary: Evaluation spans the Shepp-Logan phantom and other test images, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 embeddings from MobileNetV3, IMDB and Emotion text embeddings from BERT, and the weight matrices of LlaMa-7b.
sections.additional: For embeddings, a k-nearest-neighbor classifier measures downstream accuracy and weighted F1; matrix reconstruction quality is measured by relative Frobenius norm error under matched (parity) bit budgets across methods.
sections.audio_script: The experiments cover a deliberately diverse set of matrices. For images, the authors compress the Shepp-Logan phantom, a standard medical-imaging test image, along with a Hubble image of Jupiter and an MR brain scan. For embeddings, they use CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 image embeddings from MobileNetV3, and IMDB and Emotion text embeddings from BERT, evaluating a three-nearest-neighbor classifier by accuracy and weighted F1 score. And for large language models, they compress the weight matrices of LlaMa-7b layer by layer. Throughout, they enforce parity, giving every method the same total bit budget, and report relative Frobenius norm error alongside the task metrics.

sections.heading: Key Result
sections.necessary: LPLR compresses matrices to as low as one bit per coordinate while matching or surpassing baselines: on CIFAR-10 embeddings at Bnq = 1 bit it retains 92% accuracy (unquantized 91%) versus 11% for naive quantization, and on LlaMa-7b weights LPLR-SVD achieves 0.537 mean relative Frobenius error versus 0.836 for naive quant.
sections.additional: On the Shepp-Logan phantom LPLR shows the least visual distortion at aggressive budgets, preserving fine semantic features (the small ellipses) at an average of ~1 bit per pixel where naive 2-bit quantization visibly degrades.
sections.audio_script: The headline finding is that LPLR delivers extreme compression, down to roughly one bit per matrix coordinate, while preserving performance. On CIFAR-10 embeddings quantized to a single bit, LPLR retains ninety-two percent classification accuracy, actually matching or exceeding the unquantized ninety-one percent, whereas naive quantization collapses to eleven percent. On CIFAR-100 the gap is even starker: seventy-nine percent for LPLR versus about one percent for naive quant at one bit. And on the weight matrices of LlaMa-7b, LPLR-SVD attains a mean relative Frobenius norm error of about zero point five four, compared to zero point eight four for naive quantization, with lower variance across layers. Visually, on the Shepp-Logan phantom, LPLR preserves the fine anatomical details that competing methods wash out.

sections.heading: Ablation Study
sections.necessary: Sweeping the bit-budget triplet (B, B′, Bnq) at fixed compression ratio (Table 3) shows LPLR and LPLR-SVD steadily lower Frobenius error as the low-rank budget B shrinks and Bnq grows, outperforming naive quant in the low-Bnq regime.
sections.additional: Increasing Bnq from 1 to 4 bits moves LPLR from clearly beating direct-SVD and naive quant toward performance parity, isolating the separate contributions of low-rank structure and quantization precision.
sections.audio_script: The paper carefully separates the two effects at play, low rank structure and quantization precision, through several ablations. Table 3 sweeps the bit-budget triplet while holding the compression ratio fixed, and shows that shifting budget from the low-rank factors toward the non-quantized reference systematically lowers the Frobenius norm error for LPLR and its SVD variant. Across the embedding tables, raising the quantization budget Bnq from one bit to four bits moves LPLR from decisively beating naive and direct-SVD quantization at the aggressive end toward performance parity at the relaxed end. These sweeps confirm that LPLR's advantage is largest precisely where compression is most extreme.

sections.heading: Headline Numbers
sections.necessary: - ~1 bit per matrix coordinate compression while maintaining task performance. - CIFAR-10 embeddings, 1-bit: 92% accuracy (LPLR) vs 11% (naive quant); unquantized 91%. - CIFAR-100 embeddings, 1-bit: 79% accuracy (LPLR) vs ~1% (naive quant). - LlaMa-7b weights (B=B′=8, Bnq=4): mean relative Frobenius error 0.537 (LPLR-SVD) vs 0.836 (naive quant).
sections.additional: LPLR computational cost is O(ndm) versus O(nd²) for direct-SVD; error bound scales as (1 + k/(m−k−1))·‖A_k − A‖²_F + ε.
sections.audio_script: To put numbers on it: LPLR compresses down to about one bit per matrix coordinate. On CIFAR-10 embeddings at one bit, it holds ninety-two percent accuracy against just eleven percent for naive quantization, essentially matching the unquantized ninety-one percent. On CIFAR-100 at one bit, seventy-nine percent versus roughly one percent. On LlaMa-7b weights, a mean relative Frobenius norm error of zero point five four for the SVD variant versus zero point eight four for naive quant. And computationally, LPLR runs in order n d m time, a large saving over the order n d squared cost of computing a full singular value decomposition.

sections.heading: Takeaway
sections.necessary: Jointly exploiting low rank and low precision through a randomized Gaussian sketch, LPLR compresses matrices to roughly one bit per entry with provable error bounds, matching or beating standard compression on images, embeddings, and LLM weights at a fraction of the cost of an SVD.
sections.additional: The equalization property of Gaussian embeddings is the key enabler, keeping quantization error bounded even at 1-bit precision.
sections.audio_script: The takeaway is that low rank and low precision are complementary, and exploiting them together pays off. By sketching a matrix with a Gaussian random projection and quantizing the resulting factors, LPLR achieves compression as aggressive as one bit per coordinate while preserving accuracy on images, embeddings, and large language model weights, and it comes with upper bounds on the approximation error. Crucially, it avoids the expensive singular value decomposition, running in order n d m time, which makes it a practical option for the very largest matrices where exact methods simply do not fit.
